decisions.quote: We observed evidence for a directionality effect in the spatial gap discrimination task, as reflected in enhanced performance when moving toward as compared to moving away from the probe, which provides a replication of the previously established directionality effects in spatial tasks ( Festman et al., 2013a , b ).
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The authors explicitly predict and empirically test the movement direction effect (enhanced discrimination when moving the right hand toward versus away from the probe while the left hand remains at rest) from Festman et al. (2013b, Frontiers in Psychology 4:657, DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00657) across Experiment 1 (temporal gap discrimination) and Experiment 2 (spatial gap discrimination), explicitly stating in Results and Discussion that the spatial gap discrimination findings reproduce and provide 'a replication of the previously established directionality effects in spatial tasks ( Festman et al., 2013a , b )'. This work is absent from shipped row 2153 (Gozli, West & Pratt, 2012, DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2012.04.008), which tested static hand proximity effects, and is a distinct empirical paper from sibling target_index 1 (Festman et al., 2013a, DOI: 10.3758/s13414-013-0430-4), as described in the Introduction ('The interplay of near-hand and direction effects was examined in a subsequent study by Festman et al. (2013b) , in which the right hand moved below the display, while the left hand remained stationary on the side').

expert_decision_not_adopted.quote: Based on the MVP hypothesis, we predicted improving temporal gap discrimination and impaired spatial gap detection as the hand approached the probe as compared to when the hand moves away from the probe. Furthermore, on the basis of the direction effect of Festman et al. (2013a , b ), we predicted better discrimination when moving toward the probe in both tasks.
expert_decision_not_adopted.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The paper empirically re-tests the movement direction effect (superior visual discrimination when the hand moves toward versus away from a visual probe during continuous hand movement below the display) originally reported by Festman et al. (2013a, Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics 75:644-649, DOI: 10.3758/s13414-013-0430-4). The authors explicitly predict this direction effect in both temporal (Experiment 1) and spatial (Experiment 2) gap discrimination tasks, test Direction (toward vs. away) in their repeated-measures ANOVAs, and conclude in Results and Discussion that Experiment 2 reproduced and provided 'a replication of the previously established directionality effects in spatial tasks ( Festman et al., 2013a , b )' while Experiment 1 showed no modulation by movement direction. Shipped row 2153 (Gozli, West & Pratt, 2012, DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2012.04.008) is a different study testing static hand proximity (near vs. far) under the modulated visual pathways hypothesis, and sibling target_index 2 (Festman et al., 2013b, DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00657) is a separate subsequent empirical article examining the interplay of a stationary left hand and moving right hand.
